name: C9-5
question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.

turns.text: I'm trying to get a handle on Hong Kong's subdivided flats and the housing policy debate around them. Could you pull up some sources on that topic for me?

I don't have any documents in front of me, so I can't pull up sources — but I can help you figure out what to look for. What would a source need to do for your essay: back up a specific claim you're making, show a counter-view, define something, or give a first-hand account? And which claim would it be serving?

I want to start broad and just see what's out there on subdivided units in Hong Kong — the basic descriptive picture of who lives in them and why. Could you pull up something that gives an overview of the tenants and the housing situation?

You've said you want the basic descriptive picture — who lives in subdivided units and why. What would that description need to establish for your essay: that these tenants are a particular group, that their situation has a specific cause, or something else you're setting up?

It's for an essay where I want to set up who ends up in subdivided units and why they're there in the first place. I don't have a claim yet — I just want a source that gives me the profile of these tenants and the broader housing context they're stuck in. Something descriptive to anchor the opening.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D1: Subdivided Housing in Hong Kong: A Primer (Policy brief). Policy brief primer giving descriptive overview of SDU tenants and housing context.
- D3: Tenant Interview: Mr Chan, Kwai Chung (Interview). First-person interview with a tenant describing his living situation and views.
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case note on Berlin's rent cap, offering international perspective.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report surveying tenants and arguing for tenure security over hard caps.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling rent control effects on marginal housing supply.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
descriptive overview plus first-hand tenant account to anchor the opening
Unlocked: D1 (Subdivided Housing in Hong Kong: A Primer), D3 (Tenant Interview: Mr Chan, Kwai Chung). You can now read their passages by id, for example D1p1.

Thanks. Before I go further, I want to understand the household profile behind these units and what tenants themselves say the real problem is. Can you pull a document that surveys SDU tenants at scale — something with numbers on what they'd trade for security or a faster housing offer — and one that lays out the supply picture and any elasticity estimates? I've only looked at the primer and the interview so far.

You've said you want tenant-side numbers and a supply-side picture — but I can't pull documents, and I won't guess at any.

So tell me: for the claim you're building, what would each source need to *do* — show a pattern, give a counter-view, define a term, or carry a tenant's own account? And which claim is each one serving?

Fair. Let me be more concrete. For the tenant-side piece I want something that quantifies what households would accept in exchange for security or a faster offer — a survey with percentages. For the supply side I want elasticity estimates, ideally a range, so I can see how responsive this kind of stock is to rent. And honestly I keep circling back to the interview I already have — the tenant who talks about the waiting list — because I want to test whether his framing is idiosyncratic or representative. So: one survey document with trade-off numbers, and one document carrying supply elasticity, please.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt tracking SDU stock and rents over time, with caveats on post-2023 extrapolation.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper reviewing elasticity estimates and modeling cap scenarios.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report surveying 440 SDU households on trade-offs and policy preferences.
- D3: Tenant Interview: Mr Chan, Kwai Chung (Interview). Interview with a single tenant, offering personal experience and views.
- D7: Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021 (Comparative case). Comparative case study of Berlin's rent cap and its aftermath.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
survey trade-offs, supply elasticity, and stock data for tenant-side and supply-side claims

Unlocked: D11 (NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First), D6 (Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing), D2 (SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt)). You can now read their passages by id, for example D11p1.
tenant trade-off survey and supply elasticity paper
Unlocked: D11 (NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First), D6 (Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing). You can now read their passages by id, for example D11p1.
Berlin case study needed for comparative evidence
Unlocked: D7 (Comparative Note: Berlin, Mietendeckel 2020–2021). You can now read their passages by id, for example D7p1.
I still need the Hong Kong enforcement and legal material to round out the picture — the inspection capacity and the legal opinion on instruments. Can you surface sources on those?

You've named two things — inspection capacity and a legal opinion on instruments. Which claim in your essay is each one meant to support, and what would it need to show for that claim: evidence of how enforcement works, a counter-view, or a definition of the instruments themselves?

The inspection-capacity piece is meant to support a practical objection: that a tightened cap could not actually be enforced across the stock. The legal opinion is meant to show what instrument a careful lawyer thinks is defensible instead. For the first I'd need evidence of how much of the stock inspectors actually reach; for the second, a definition of the instruments and their legal footing.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Landlord association submission, owner vantage, concedes no margin data and self-reported survey limits.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper reviewing elasticity literature and distinguishing first- from second-generation controls.
- D10: Internal Minute: Housing Authority Enforcement Subcommittee (draft, not for circulation) (Internal minute). Internal enforcement subcommittee minute, draft not for circulation, on inspection capacity and register feasibility.
- D9: Legal Opinion: Compensation and Judicial Review Risk (Legal opinion). Legal opinion assessing compensation and judicial review risk, proposing a band-based middle instrument.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report surveying tenant preferences, arguing caps treat price symptom of quantity problem.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
Enforcement capacity and legal instrument footing

Unlocked: D10 (Internal Minute: Housing Authority Enforcement Subcommittee (draft, not for circulation)), D9 (Legal Opinion: Compensation and Judicial Review Risk). You can now read their passages by id, for example D10p1.

I think I've got what I need from those two. Let me pull the remaining thread together — I want to check one last source before I try to write anything, something that speaks to the landlord side and the actual margin economics, since I keep hearing that owners can't absorb anything.

You've said you want the landlord side and the margin economics, and that you keep hearing owners can't absorb anything. What would that source need to show for your essay — a counter-view to that claim, hard evidence on the numbers, or a landlord's own account?

Something with the landlord's own account would be ideal — someone who actually owns and lets these units, saying in plain terms what they can and can't absorb, so I can test the claim that owners can't take any cut at all against a real voice rather than a slogan.

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Statistical index excerpt giving aggregate stock and rent trends, with a voluntary-reporting caveat.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report speaking for tenants, opposing hard caps and favoring tenure security.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling supply elasticity and welfare effects of rent caps.
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Landlord association submission giving owners' own account, but conceding no margin data.
- D9: Legal Opinion: Compensation and Judicial Review Risk (Legal opinion). Legal opinion assessing compensation and judicial review risk of a hard initial-rent cap.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
